title: A First Look at WinDbg
summary: **WinDbg** is Microsoft's command-line-driven debugger. It does everything Visual Studio's debugger does and much more, opens any crash dump, and is the only debugger for the Windows kernel (chapter 16). This lesson installs it and teaches the two dozen commands that cover nearly all everyday work, mapped to the Visual Studio windows you already know.
markdown:
## Why another debugger

Visual Studio's debugger is the most comfortable way to debug your own code. WinDbg is worth knowing because:

- it opens crash dumps from anywhere, quickly, with `!analyze` summarising them;
- it can debug programs and machines where Visual Studio is not installed;
- it has powerful commands for heaps, handles, locks and Windows internals;
- it is **the** kernel debugger: chapters 15 and 16 depend on it.

Install **WinDbg** from the Microsoft Store (search "WinDbg"; older guides call the new version "WinDbg Preview"). It has a modern window with source, locals and call stack panes, but its heart is the **command window**.

## Getting started

- **File → Launch executable** to start a program under the debugger, **Attach to process** for a running one, or **Open dump file** for a `.dmp`.
- First, set up symbols (lesson 8.02):

```
.symfix C:\Symbols          ; use Microsoft's symbol server, caching in C:\Symbols
.sympath+ C:\code\game\x64\Debug   ; add your own PDB folder
.reload                     ; load symbols with the new path
```

## The everyday commands

| Task | WinDbg | Visual Studio equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| Continue | `g` | F5 |
| Step over / into | `p` / `t` | F10 / F11 |
| Step out | `gu` | Shift+F11 |
| Breakpoint on a function | `bp game!Player::update` | F9 |
| Breakpoint on a source line | `bp `` `main.cpp:42` `` ` (with backticks) | F9 |
| List / clear breakpoints | `bl` / `bc *` | Breakpoints window |
| Data breakpoint: break on write to 4 bytes | `ba w4 0x0000004f8c8ff8a0` | Lesson 4.09 |
| Call stack | `k` (`kp` with parameters, `kn` numbered) | Call Stack |
| Switch to frame n | `.frame n` | Double-click a frame |
| Locals | `dv` (`dv /t` with types) | Locals |
| Show a typed object | `dt game!Player 0x...` or `dt player` | Watch |
| Registers | `r` (`r rax` for one) | Registers |
| Memory as bytes / dwords / qwords | `db addr` / `dd addr` / `dq addr` | Memory window |
| Memory as text | `da addr` (ASCII), `du addr` (UTF-16) | Memory window, text column |
| Disassemble | `u addr` (`uf function` for the whole function) | Disassembly |
| Loaded modules | `lm` (`lmvm game` for details) | Modules |
| Threads | `~` (`~2s` switches to thread 2; `~*k` stacks of all threads) | Threads |
| Evaluate an expression | `? rsp + 0x20` | Watch |
| Help | `.hh command` | |

Commands that start with `.` are debugger meta-commands; those starting with `!` are **extensions**, larger commands supplied by DLLs loaded into the debugger.

## Analysing a crash dump

Open a dump from lesson 8.04 and run:

```
!analyze -v
```

It reads the exception record, finds the faulting thread and frame, applies heuristics, and prints a summary:

```
EXCEPTION_CODE: (NTSTATUS) 0xc0000005 - The instruction at 0x7ff6a1235f10 referenced memory at 0x10.
                                        The memory could not be read.
FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE:  C:\code\game\inventory.cpp
FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE_NUMBER:  42
STACK_TEXT:
game!Inventory::totalWeight+0x20
game!Hud::drawWeight+0x45
game!Hud::draw+0x9a
...
```

Then dig in with `k`, `.frame`, `dv` and `dt` as in a live session. `.ecxr` switches the debugger's context to the moment of the exception (the registers when it happened), which matters for dumps where the current context is the crash handler.

## Useful extensions

| Command | Shows |
|---|---|
| `!heap -s` | Summary of the process heaps |
| `!handle` | Open handles and their types (spotting handle leaks, lesson 5.01) |
| `!locks` | Critical sections that are held, and by which thread (deadlocks, lesson 8.07) |
| `!peb` | The process environment block: command line, environment, loaded modules |
| `!address addr` | What kind of memory an address is in (lesson 6.04's `VirtualQuery`, done for you) |

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Forgetting symbols
> Without `.symfix` and your PDB path, everything is addresses. Fix symbols before anything else.

> [!warning] Reading a dump's stack without `.ecxr`
> You may be looking at the crash handler's stack instead of the crash.

> [!warning] Typing `g` by habit in a dump
> A dump is not running: it cannot continue. Use the inspection commands.

## Knowledge check

```quiz
? Which WinDbg command shows the call stack?
+ `k`
- `g`
- `lm`
> `kp` adds parameters, `kn` frame numbers.

? What does `!analyze -v` do?
+ Reads the exception in a dump or broken-in process and summarises the likely cause, faulting frame and stack
- Lists all modules
- Steps one instruction
> It is the usual first command on a crash dump.

? How do you look at the 4-byte values at an address?
+ `dd address`
- `db address`
- `du address`
> `db` shows bytes, `dd` double words (4 bytes), `dq` quad words, `du` UTF-16 text.

? What does `.symfix` do?
+ Points the symbol path at Microsoft's public symbol server
- Fixes corrupted PDB files
- Removes all symbols
> Follow it with `.reload`.
```
ideas:
- Open a crash dump from lesson 8.04 in WinDbg, run `.symfix`, `.reload`, `!analyze -v`, then `.ecxr` and `k`.
- Launch one of your programs under WinDbg, set `bp` on a function, and use `dv` and `dt` when it stops.
- Run `lm` and compare the list with Visual Studio's Modules window.

cards.q: Why learn WinDbg when Visual Studio has a debugger?
cards.a: It analyses crash dumps quickly, works where Visual Studio is not installed, has deep Windows-specific commands, and is the debugger used for the kernel.

cards.q: What is the difference between commands starting with `.` and with `!`?
cards.a: `.` commands control the debugger itself; `!` commands are extensions provided by debugger DLLs.

cards.q: Which commands show locals, a typed structure and raw memory?
cards.a: `dv` for locals, `dt` for a typed structure, and `db`/`dd`/`dq` for memory as bytes, dwords or qwords.
